summary: Describes the problem statement for Configuration and Provisioning for Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP), the need to configure and manage many wireless access points centrally.

eli5.summary: A school with lots of wifi boxes wants to set them all up from one place. This memo explains why that is a problem to solve.

questions: why is managing many wifi boxes hard
subtitle: Managing thousands of wireless access points from one place

tldr.problem: Large deployments of wireless LANs require managing many individual access points, each needing separate configuration and monitoring, which strains network administration resources.
tldr.mechanism: A standardized architecture with centralized controllers managing distributed access points, rather than individual APs managing themselves.
tldr.outcome: This problem statement identified the need for standardized protocols, leading to the CAPWAP protocol development.

today: RFC 3990 is an Informational document describing the problems that motivated CAPWAP development. The actual CAPWAP protocol was developed subsequently.

sections.title: The Wireless Explosion
sections.content: When the IEEE approved faster wireless standards (802.11a and 802.11b) in 1999, increasing speeds to 11 and 54 Mbps, enterprises began deploying wireless LANs at scale. Large deployments grew to thousands of access points. Unlike wired networks where one device might handle many ports, each wireless access point (AP) is a separate IP device requiring its own management and configuration.
sections.eli5: WiFi got faster in 1999, so companies wanted to install lots of access points. But each AP is its own device that needs separate attention.

sections.title: The Problems at Scale
sections.content: Four main problems emerge with large WLAN deployments. First, each AP doubles the network infrastructure to manage, burdening network administrators. Second, distributing consistent configuration across hundreds of APs is difficult, mixing both static settings (addressing and hardware) with dynamic parameters (WLAN settings and security). Third, the shared wireless medium requires constant monitoring and coordination across all APs to minimize interference and optimize performance. Fourth, security risks increase because APs must be placed in hard-to-secure locations outside locked closets, creating risks of theft and unauthorized access.
sections.eli5: Managing many APs is hard because they need the same settings everywhere, they all affect each other on the wireless channel, and they are often in places thieves can steal them.

sections.title: The Centralized Solution
sections.content: Vendors began offering proprietary solutions combining centralized control with distributed access points. The RFC proposes a standardized architecture with two components: many 802.11 access points (APs) and one or more central control devices called access controllers (ACs). With an interoperable standard, network designers could choose different vendors for APs and controllers independently, rather than being locked to proprietary solutions.
sections.eli5: Instead of many separate boxes, have a few central control offices that run the show, and simpler access points that just do what they are told.
